definition: Error that arises because some members of the target population are not represented on the sampling frame (or the frame holds ineligible or duplicate units): the discrepancy between target and frame population.
Error from measuring a sample rather than the whole frame population: the variation of estimates over possible samples under the design, plus any bias from the selection mechanism.
Error that occurs after sampling when sampled units do not respond, or skip items, and respondents differ from nonrespondents on the survey variable.
Error that arises because of errors in post-survey weighting: poorly chosen adjustment variables, extreme weights, or wrong population controls.
Error when the construct the question measures differs from the construct the analysis needs; a gap between the concept and what is asked (validity of the measure).
Deviation of the reported value from the true value, from respondents, interviewers, the instrument or the mode.
Error introduced after collection by coding, editing, data entry, cleaning or matching; random when procedures vary (coders disagree), systematic when they consistently change values.
Error in the analysis itself: estimation ignoring weights or design, wrong software options, misleading language, or unreported quality (West et al. 2017).
Error in found data from who appears in the source: the units generating the data differ from the target population and are not selected by design.
Error from matching or linking found data to other records or surveys: units unmatched, mismatched or wrongly merged.
Error in found data produced by the platform or algorithm generating it: system changes, suggested terms or algorithmic confounding that alter what is recorded.
The passage concerns no particular survey error source.

Simple random sampling: every sample of size n from the frame has the same chance of selection.
Systematic sampling: a random start and then every k-th unit from an ordered list.
Stratified sampling: the frame is divided into strata and a sample is drawn independently in each.
Cluster sampling: groups of elements (clusters, PSUs) are selected and all or some elements in them observed.
Multistage sampling: units selected in stages, e.g. PSUs, then SSUs within them, then elements.
Probability proportional to size: units selected with probability proportional to a measure of size.
Two-phase (double) sampling: a first-phase sample measures auxiliary variables used to select or adjust a second-phase subsample.
Nonprobability samples: opt-in panels, quota, convenience or found data without known selection probabilities.
